source_text: Ante omnia pacis doctor adque unitatis magister singillatim noluit et priuatim precem fieri, ut quis cum precatur pro se tantum precetur. non dicimus: pater meus, qui es in caelis nec: panem meum da mihi hodie, nec dimitti sibi tantum unusquisque debitum postulat aut ut in temptationem non inducatur adque a malo liberetur pro se solo rogat. publica est nobis et communis oratio, et quando oramus, non pro uno sed pro populo toto oramus, quia totus populus unum sumus. Deus pacis et concordiae magister qui docuit unitatem, sic orare unum pro omnibus uoluit, quomodo in uno omnes ipse portauit. hanc orationis legem seruauerunt tres pueri in camino ignis inclusi consonantes in prece et spiritus consensione concordes: declarat scripturae diuinae fides et dum docet quomodo orauerint tales, dat exemplum quod imitari in precibus debeamus, ut tales esse possimus. tunc inquit, illi tres tamquam ex uno ore hymnum canebant et benedicebant Deum. loquebantur quasi ex uno ore, et nondum illos Christus docuerat orare. et idcirco orantibus fuit inpetrabilis et efficax sermo, quia promerebatur Dominum pacifica et simplex et spiritalis oratio. sic. et apostolos cum discipulis post ascensum Domini inuenimus orasse. erant, inquit, perseuerantes omnes unanimes in oratione cum mulieribus et Maria quae fuerat mater Iesu et fratribus eius. perseuerabant in oratione unanimes orationis suae et instantia simul et concordia declarantes, quia Deus qui inhabitare facit unanimes in domo non admittit in diuinam et aeternam domum nisi aput quos est unanimis oratio.
orientation: Cyprian is explaining why the Lord's Prayer uses 'our' rather than 'my,' grounding this in the unity of the whole people of God.
pass_a_gloss: Before all things the teacher of peace and master of unity did not want prayer to be made one by one and privately, so that anyone when he prays should pray for himself only. We do not say: my Father, who are in heaven, nor: give me my bread today, nor does each one ask that debt be forgiven for himself only or ask that he not be led into temptation and be freed from evil for himself alone. The prayer is public and common for us, and when we pray, we pray not for one but for the whole people, because the whole people are one. God, the teacher of peace and concord, who taught unity, wanted one to pray for all in this way, just as he himself carried all in one. The three boys shut in the furnace of fire kept this law of prayer, harmonious in prayer and in agreement of spirit concordant: the faith of the divine scripture declares this, and while it teaches how such ones prayed, it gives an example which we ought to imitate in prayers, so that we may be able to be such. Then, it says, those three as if from one mouth were singing a hymn and blessing God. They were speaking as if from one mouth, and Christ had not yet taught them to pray. And therefore for those praying the speech was obtainable and effective, because a peaceful and simple and spiritual prayer was winning the Lord. So. And we find the apostles with the disciples after the ascension of the Lord to have prayed. They were, it says, all persevering with one mind in prayer with the women and Mary who had been the mother of Jesus and his brothers. They were persevering in prayer with one mind, declaring by the urgency and at the same time the concord of their prayer, because God who makes those of one mind dwell in a house does not admit into the divine and eternal house except those among whom prayer is of one mind.

choices.english: teacher of peace and master of unity
choices.why: Keeps the two titles parallel and literal; 'doctor' and 'magister' are distinct nouns in the source.
rejected: instructor of peace and teacher of unity

choices.term: publica est nobis et communis oratio
choices.english: The prayer is public and common for us
choices.why: Preserves the two adjectives 'publica' and 'communis' and the dative of reference 'nobis'.
rejected: our prayer is public and shared

choices.why: 'Promereor' means to earn or win favor; the object 'Dominum' is the Lord whose favor is won, not a vocative of address.

choices.english: the speech was obtainable and effective
choices.why: Keeps the two adjectives as predicates of 'sermo' and renders 'inpetrabilis' literally as 'obtainable' (able to obtain what is asked).
rejected: the prayer was heard and powerful

choices.why: Renders the adjective 'unanimis' modifying 'oratio' literally, preserving the unity theme.

pass_b_english: Above all, the teacher of peace and master of unity did not want prayer to be made one by one and privately, so that when someone prays he prays only for himself. We do not say, “My Father, who are in heaven,” nor “Give me my bread today.” No one asks that his debt be forgiven for himself alone, or begs for himself alone not to be led into temptation and to be delivered from evil. The prayer is public and common for us, and when we pray, we pray not for one person but for the whole people, because the whole people are one. God, the teacher of peace and concord who taught unity, wanted one to pray for all in this way, just as he himself carried all in the one. The three children shut inside the fiery furnace kept this law of prayer, harmonious in their petition and united in the agreement of the Spirit. The witness of divine Scripture makes this clear, and while it teaches how they prayed, it gives us an example to imitate in our prayers, so that we may be able to be like them. “Then,” it says, “those three were singing a hymn as if from one mouth and blessing God” (Daniel 3:51). They spoke as if from one mouth, and Christ had not yet taught them to pray. And so their speech earned the Lord's favor and was effective for them as they prayed, because a peaceful, simple, and spiritual prayer deserved the Lord's response. In the same way we find that the apostles prayed with the disciples after the Lord’s ascension. “They were all persevering with one mind in prayer,” it says, “with the women and Mary, who had been the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” (Acts 1:14). They were persevering in prayer with one mind, showing by their urgency and their unity together that God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house, does not admit anyone into the divine and eternal house except where there is unanimous prayer.

problems.why: 'Promerebatur' means 'earned/deserved' (from promereri), not 'winning' in the sense of charming or gaining advantage over. The prayer deserved the Lord's response.
'Inpetrabilis' means 'obtainable/answered' in the sense of 'successful in obtaining,' but 'obtainable' suggests the speech itself could be obtained, not that it successfully obtained God's favor.
problems.fix: their speech won God's favor and was effective
problems.ruling: 'inpetrabilis' means 'able to obtain (from God)'; 'obtainable' reverses direction, implying the speech is obtainable.

edits.old: their speech was obtainable and effective for them as they prayed, because a peaceful, simple, and spiritual prayer was winning the Lord.
edits.new: their speech earned the Lord's favor and was effective for them as they prayed, because a peaceful, simple, and spiritual prayer deserved the Lord's response.

fixed: Changed 'obtainable' and 'winning the Lord' to reflect 'inpetrabilis' as successful in obtaining and 'promerebatur' as earned/deserved: 'their speech earned the Lord's favor and was effective... because a peaceful, simple, and spiritual prayer deserved the Lord's response.'

problems.quote: does not admit anyone into the divine and eternal house except those whose prayer is of one mind
problems.source_quote: non admittit in diuinam et aeternam domum nisi aput quos est unanimis oratio
problems.why: The Latin says God does not admit anyone into his house except those among whom there is unanimous prayer; 'except those whose prayer is of one mind' changes the condition from communal presence to individual possession.
problems.fix: does not admit anyone into the divine and eternal house except where there is unanimous prayer.
problems.ruling: aput quos est = 'among whom'; shifts from communal shared prayer to individual possessive 'whose prayer'.

edits.old: does not admit anyone into the divine and eternal house except those whose prayer is of one mind
edits.new: does not admit anyone into the divine and eternal house except where there is unanimous prayer

fixed: Changed 'except those whose prayer is of one mind' to 'except where there is unanimous prayer' because the Latin 'nisi aput quos est unanimis oratio' means 'except among whom there is unanimous prayer,' a communal condition, not an individual possession.

last_rejected.quote: just as he himself carried all in the one
last_rejected.source_quote: quomodo in uno omnes ipse portauit
last_rejected.why: 'In uno' means 'in the one' (i.e., in one person/Adam), not 'in the one' as a vague referent; the sense is that God carried all in one (man).
last_rejected.fix: just as he himself bore all in the one
last_rejected.ruling: 'in uno' = 'in the one' is standard translation; 'one' as antecedent is clear from context of unity theme.

last_rejected.quote: so that when someone prays he prays only for himself
last_rejected.source_quote: ut quis cum precatur pro se tantum precetur
last_rejected.why: English adds 'when someone prays' as a general statement, but Latin 'cum precatur' is temporal 'when he prays.' The English 'so that...he prays only for himself' changes the purpose: Latin says 'he did not want prayer to be made singly and privately, so that [with the result that] when someone prays, he prays only for himself.' The English 'so that when someone prays he prays only for himself' is slightly ambiguous but conveys the same meaning. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter's own claim says 'No error'; English conveys same meaning as Latin 'ut quis cum precatur pro se tantum precetur'.

last_rejected.why: Latin 'unum sumus' = 'we are one'; English 'are one' changes 'we' to 'the whole people are one'—this loses the first-person 'we.' The subject is 'totus populus' = 'the whole people,' and 'sumus' = 'we are.' So 'the whole people are one' is grammatically odd (collective noun with plural verb) but 'the whole people we are one' would be wrong. Actually 'totus populus unum sumus' = 'the whole people, we are one' or 'we, the whole people, are one.' English 'the whole people are one' loses the 'we.' This is a minor omission of the first-person identification.
last_rejected.fix: the whole people, we are one
last_rejected.ruling: 'totus populus unum sumus' rendered as 'the whole people are one'; first-person 'we' is implicit in collective subject, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: their speech earned the Lord's favor and was effective for them as they prayed, because a peaceful, simple, and spiritual prayer deserved the Lord's response
last_rejected.source_quote: orantibus fuit inpetrabilis et efficax sermo, quia promerebatur Dominum pacifica et simplex et spiritalis oratio
last_rejected.why: Winning the Lord is moved from the prayer onto the speech, and Dominum becomes a response owed.
last_rejected.fix: And so, as they prayed, their words prevailed and were effective, because a peaceful, simple, and spiritual prayer was winning the Lord.
last_rejected.ruling: "promerebatur Dominum" means 'deserved/won the Lord'; "earned the Lord's favor"/"deserved the Lord's response" stays within range, and the subject remains the prayer; no meaning lost.
